L9.D21.label: §2.1 Definition 2.1
L9.D21.text: $S\subseteq T$ is **upper bounded** if $\exists u\in T$ with $s\le u$ for all $s\in S$ ($u$ is an upper bound); **lower bounded** if $\exists l\in T$ with $l\le s$ for all $s\in S$; **bounded** if both.

L9.R1.label: §2.1 Remark 1
L9.R1.text: Anything above an upper bound is an upper bound; anything below a lower bound is a lower bound.

L9.D22.label: §2.1 Definition 2.2
L9.D22.text: $u^*$ is the **supremum** (least upper bound) of $S$ if $u^*$ is an upper bound and $u^*\le u$ for every upper bound $u$. The **infimum** $l^*$ is a lower bound with $l\le l^*$ for every lower bound $l$.

L9.P21.label: §2.1 Proposition 2.1
L9.P21.text: If $S$ has a supremum, it is unique.

L9.E21.label: §2.1 Example 2.1
L9.E21.text: $H_+=\{\tfrac1n : n\in\mathbb N\}\subseteq\mathbb Q$. Prove $\sup H_+=1$ in two steps: 1 is an upper bound, and every upper bound $u$ has $1\le u$.

L9.R2.label: §2.1 Remark 2
L9.R2.text: Here the supremum $1$ is an element of $H_+$.

L9.E22.label: §2.1 Example 2.2
L9.E22.text: $H_-=\{-\tfrac1n : n\in\mathbb N\}$. Prove $\sup H_-=0$ in two steps.

L9.R3.label: §2.1 Remark 3
L9.R3.text: Here the supremum $0$ is in $\mathbb Q$ but **not** in $H_-$.

L9.D23.label: §2.1 Definition 2.3
L9.D23.text: If $\sup S\in S$ it is the **maximum** $\max S$; if $\inf S\in S$ it is the **minimum** $\min S$.

L9.D24.label: §2.1 Definition 2.4
L9.D24.text: A totally ordered set $T$ is **complete** if every nonempty upper bounded subset has a supremum in $T$.

L9.D25.label: §2.1 Definition 2.5
L9.D25.text: An ordered field is a **complete ordered field** if every nonempty upper bounded subset has a supremum in it.

L9.R4.label: §2.1 Remark 4
L9.R4.text: Completeness is a property of the total order; it doesn't need the field structure.

L9.R5.label: §2.1 Remark 5
L9.R5.text: In a complete totally ordered set, every nonempty lower bounded subset has an infimum. Why?

L9.R6.label: §2.2 Remark 6
L9.R6.text: The diagonal of a unit square has length $x$ with $x^2=2$, so some lengths are not rational.

L9.T22.label: §2.2 Theorem 2.2
L9.T22.text: $\mathbb Q$ is not complete: $S=\{x\in\mathbb Q: x>0,\ x^2<2\}$ is nonempty and upper bounded but has no supremum in $\mathbb Q$.

L9.T23.label: §2.2 Theorem 2.3
L9.T23.text: There is a unique (up to isomorphism) complete ordered field $(\mathbb R,+,\cdot,<)$, and it contains a copy of $\mathbb Q$.

L9.CA.label: §2.2 Completeness axiom
L9.CA.text: **Completeness axiom.** Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is upper bounded has a supremum.

L9.R7.label: §2.2 Remark 7
L9.R7.text: 'Unique up to isomorphism': any complete ordered field $F_1$ has a bijection $g:F_1\to\mathbb R$ preserving $+$, $\cdot$ and $<$.

L9.T24.label: §2.2 Theorem 2.4
L9.T24.text: There is a unique positive $x\in\mathbb R$ with $x^2=2$.

L9.R8.label: §2.2 Remark 8
L9.R8.text: So $\sqrt2\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$: irrational numbers exist.

L10.P11.label: §1 Proposition 1.1 (template)
L10.P11.text: Template for $u^*=\sup S$: (i) show $s\le u^*$ for all $s\in S$; (ii) show $u^*\le u$ for every upper bound $u$, **or** show any $u<u^*$ is not an upper bound.

L10.P21.label: §2 Proposition 2.1
L10.P21.text: For $S$ nonempty, upper bounded: $u^*=\sup S$ iff (a) $u^*$ is an upper bound and (b) $\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists x\in S$ with $x>u^*-\varepsilon$.

L10.GM.label: §2 Geometric meaning
L10.GM.text: Every window $(u^*-\varepsilon,u^*]$ just left of the sup contains a point of $S$: $S\cap(u^*-\varepsilon,u^*]\ne\varnothing$.

L10.R1.label: §2 Remark 1
L10.R1.text: A supremum can be approximated arbitrarily well by elements of the set, e.g. $\sup(0,1)=1$.

L10.R2.label: §2 Remark 2
L10.R2.text: State the analogous $\varepsilon$-characterization of the infimum.

L10.R3.label: §2 Remark 3 (nested quantifiers)
L10.R3.text: $\forall x\,\exists y\,P(x,y)$ (y may depend on x) is different from $\exists y\,\forall x\,P(x,y)$ (one y for all x).

L10.T31.label: §3 Theorem 3.1
L10.T31.text: $\mathbb N$ is not upper bounded in $\mathbb R$.

L10.T32.label: §3 Theorem 3.2 (Archimedean)
L10.T32.text: For $\varepsilon>0$ and $a\in\mathbb R$ there is $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\varepsilon>a$.

L10.T33.label: §3 Theorem 3.3
L10.T33.text: For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $n\in\mathbb N$ with $0<\tfrac1n<\varepsilon$.

L10.T41.label: §4 Theorem 4.1 (integer part)
L10.T41.text: For every $x\in\mathbb R$ there is a unique $m\in\mathbb Z$ with $m\le x<m+1$.

L10.T42.label: §4 Theorem 4.2 (density of Q)
L10.T42.text: If $x<y$ there is $q\in\mathbb Q$ with $x<q<y$ (take $q=([nx]+1)/n$ with $n(y-x)>1$).

L10.Q.label: §4 closing Question
L10.Q.text: Are the irrationals also dense on the real line?

L11.S1.label: §1 Motivation: $x^2=-1$
L11.S1.text: No real $x$ has $x^2=-1$; with $i^2=-1$ every real quadratic can be solved.

L11.S2.label: §2 Interlude: algebraically closed
L11.S2.text: $\mathbb N\subsetneq\mathbb Z\subsetneq\mathbb Q\subsetneq\mathbb R\subsetneq\mathbb C$. Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: every nonconstant complex polynomial has a root in $\mathbb C$, so $\mathbb C$ is **algebraically closed**.

L11.R1.label: §4 Remark 1
L11.R1.text: Componentwise multiplication fails: $(1,0)(0,1)=(0,0)$ with neither factor zero.

L11.R2.label: §4 Remark 2
L11.R2.text: Any field containing $\mathbb R$ and $j$ with $j^2=-1$ contains every $x+yj$.

L11.P42.label: §4 Proposition 4.2
L11.P42.text: No order makes $\mathbb C$ an ordered field ($i^2>0$ would give $-1>0$).

L11.D51.label: §5 Definition 5.1 (Fig. 3)
L11.D51.text: Conjugate $\bar z=x-iy$: reflection across the real axis.

L11.R3.label: §5 Remark 3
L11.R3.text: For real $r$, the modulus equals the absolute value $\sqrt{r^2}$.

L11.R4.label: §5 Remark 4
L11.R4.text: $z\bar z=|z|^2$, so $\frac1z=\frac{\bar z}{|z|^2}$: divide by multiplying by the conjugate.

L11.PR.label: §5 Properties (i)–(xii)
L11.PR.text: $\bar{\bar z}=z$, $\overline{z+w}=\bar z+\bar w$, $z+\bar z=2\operatorname{Re}z$, $\overline{zw}=\bar z\bar w$, $\overline{z/w}=\bar z/\bar w$, $z=\bar z\iff z\in\mathbb R$, $|\bar z|=|z|$, $z\bar z=|z|^2$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|\operatorname{Re}z|,|\operatorname{Im}z|\le|z|$, (xii) $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$.

L12.PR.label: §1 Proofs of (i)–(xi)
L12.PR.text: Proofs of the conjugate and modulus properties (i)–(xi), e.g. $|zw|^2=zw\,\bar z\bar w=|z|^2|w|^2$.

L12.R1.label: §2 Remark 1
L12.R1.text: Arguments are defined up to $2\pi k$; these notes use $[0,2\pi)$.

L12.R2.label: §2 Remark 2
L12.R2.text: $\tan\theta=\operatorname{Im}z/\operatorname{Re}z$ doesn't determine $\theta$; $\tan^{-1}$ only works when $\operatorname{Re}z>0$. Check the quadrant.

L12.ADD.label: §3 Parallelogram rule
L12.ADD.text: Addition in $\mathbb C$ is vector addition (parallelogram rule).

L12.QI.label: §3 Question (multiply by i)
L12.QI.text: What is the effect of multiplying $z$ by $i$?

L12.X31.label: §3 Exercise 3.1
L12.X31.text: Find $i^n$ by the remainder of $n$ mod 4; plot $i^0,\dots,i^7$.

L12.D41.label: §4 Definition 4.1
L12.D41.text: $z$ is an $n$th root of unity if $z^n=1$.

L12.GI.label: §4 Geometric interpretation
L12.GI.text: The roots are equally spaced on the unit circle (angle $2\pi/n$), vertices of a regular $n$-gon.

L12.X41.label: §4 Exercise 4.1
L12.X41.text: Find and plot the third roots of unity; why an equilateral triangle?

L13.D11.label: §1 Definition 1.1
L13.D11.text: $|x|=x$ if $x\ge0$, $-x$ if $x<0$, in any ordered field.

L13.R11.label: §1 Remarks 1.1–1.2
L13.R11.text: $0$ and $-x$ are the field's additive identity and inverse; $|x|\in F$.

L13.D21.label: §2 Definition 2.1 (metric)
L13.D21.text: A **metric** $d$: positivity, symmetry, triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.

L13.E21.label: §2 Example 2.1
L13.E21.text: $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ is the usual metric on $\mathbb R$.

L13.R21.label: §2 Remark 2.1
L13.R21.text: The ball depends on the metric: write $B_d(z,r)$, $D_d(z,r)$.

L13.E23.label: §2 Example 2.3
L13.E23.text: In $\mathbb R$: $B(3,1)=(2,4)$. In $\mathbb C$: picture of $B(1+i,1)$.

L13.D23.label: §2 Definition 2.3 (open set)
L13.D23.text: $U$ is open if $\forall x\in U\ \exists\varepsilon>0$ with $B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq U$.

L13.E24.label: §2 Example 2.4
L13.E24.text: $(a,b)$ open; unions of open intervals open; $[1,2)$ not open; closed disc $D$ not open.

L13.P21.label: §2 Proposition 2.1
L13.P21.text: Every open set is a union of open balls.

L13.P22.label: §2 Proposition 2.2
L13.P22.text: Any union of open sets is open; a finite intersection of open sets is open.

L13.R22.label: §2 Remark 2.2
L13.R22.text: $\varnothing$ and $S$ are open; $\bigcap_n(-\frac1n,\frac1n)=\{0\}$ is not open.

L13.D24.label: §2 Definition 2.4 (closed set)
L13.D24.text: $C$ is closed if $S\setminus C$ is open.

L13.P23.label: §2 Proposition 2.3 (Fig. 1)
L13.P23.text: An open ball is open: for $z\in B(c,r)$ use $\varepsilon=r-d(z,c)$.

L13.MAN.label: §2 Same points, different distances
L13.MAN.text: Manhattan distance $|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|$: its unit ball is a diamond.

L13.X21.label: §2 Exercise 2.1 (discrete metric)
L13.X21.text: Discrete metric: show it's a metric, describe its balls, every set is open and closed.

L13.R23.label: §2 Remark 2.3
L13.R23.text: In $\mathbb R$ with the usual metric only $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb R$ are both open and closed.

L13.E31.label: §3 Example 3.1
L13.E31.text: The modulus is a norm on $\mathbb C$.

L13.E32.label: §3 Example 3.2
L13.E32.text: The absolute value is a norm on $\mathbb R$.

L13.P31.label: §3 Proposition 3.1
L13.P31.text: A norm induces a metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (uses $\|1\|=\|-1\|=1$ for symmetry).

L14.D11.label: §1 Definition 1.1
L14.D11.text: A sequence is a function $a:\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$, $a_n=a(n)$.

L14.R1.label: §1 Remark 1
L14.R1.text: A sequence needn't have a nice formula.

L14.D13.label: §1 Definition 1.3
L14.D13.text: Sum, difference, product, quotient ($b_n\ne0$) and scalar multiple of sequences, term by term.

L14.R2.label: §1 Remark 2
L14.R2.text: $(-1)^n$ has range $\{-1,1\}$; different sequences can share a range.

L14.D15.label: §1 Definition 1.5
L14.D15.text: A **tail** is $(a_m,a_{m+1},\dots)$; e.g. $(5,6,7,\dots)$ is a tail of $a_n=n$.

L14.D21.label: §2 Definition 2.1
L14.D21.text: $a_n\to a$ if $\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists n_0(\varepsilon)$ with $|a_n-a|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge n_0(\varepsilon)$.

L14.R4.label: §2 Remark 4
L14.R4.text: $n_0$ depends on $\varepsilon$: a game against an opponent picking smaller $\varepsilon$.

L14.R5.label: §2 Remark 5
L14.R5.text: Only finitely many terms ($a_1,\dots,a_{n_0-1}$) can lie outside $B(a,\varepsilon)$.

L14.R7.label: §2 Remark 7
L14.R7.text: Find $n_0$ by working backwards on scratch paper: $\frac1n<\varepsilon\iff n>\frac1\varepsilon$.

L14.D31.label: §3 Definition 3.1
L14.D31.text: $(a_n)$ **diverges** if $\forall a\in\mathbb C\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall n_0\ \exists n\ge n_0:\ |a_n-a|\ge\varepsilon$.

L14.X31.label: §3 Exercise 3.1
L14.X31.text: $a_n\not\to a$ iff some $\varepsilon>0$ has infinitely many terms with $|a_n-a|\ge\varepsilon$.

L14.E31.label: §3 Example 3.1
L14.E31.text: $(-1)^n$ diverges: take $\varepsilon=1$; $a$ is at distance $\ge1$ from $1$ or $-1$.

L14.R8.label: §3 Remark 8 (Fig. 4)
L14.R8.text: No point is close to both $1$ and $-1$.

L14.T41.label: §4 Theorem 4.1
L14.T41.text: A convergent sequence has a unique limit (use $\varepsilon/2$ and the triangle inequality).

L15.D11.label: §1 Definition 1.1
L15.D11.text: $(a_n)$ is bounded if $\exists M>0$ with $|a_n|\le M$ for all $n$.

L15.R11.label: §1 Remarks 1.1–1.2
L15.R11.text: Equivalent: $\{|a_n|\}$ upper bounded; terms lie in $[-M,M]$ or $D(0,M)$.

L15.R13.label: §1 Remark 1.3
L15.R13.text: The converse fails: $(-1)^n$ is bounded but diverges.

L15.T21.label: §2 Theorem 2.1 (Comparison)
L15.T21.text: If $a_n\to a$, $b_n\to b$ and $a_n\le b_n$ eventually, then $a\le b$.

L15.R21.label: §2 Remark 2.1
L15.R21.text: Strict inequalities aren't preserved: $0<\frac1n$ but both limits are $0$.

L15.T22.label: §2 Theorem 2.2 (Squeeze)
L15.T22.text: $a_n\le b_n\le c_n$ eventually and $a_n,c_n\to L$ imply $b_n\to L$.

L15.P3X.label: §3 Propositions 3.1–3.8
L15.P3X.text: $a_n\to a\iff a_n-a\to0\iff|a_n-a|\to0$; $|a_n|\to|a|$; limits of sums, products, powers, quotients ($b\ne0$), $k$th roots.

L15.D41.label: §4 Definition 4.1
L15.D41.text: $a_n\to\infty$ if $\forall M>0\ \exists N(M)$ with $a_n\ge M$ for $n\ge N(M)$.

L16.R12.label: §1 Remarks 1.2–1.4
L16.R12.text: Choosing $n_0$ backwards; case (iv) from case (ii); a logarithm approach.

L16.R3X.label: §3 Remarks 3.1–3.3
L16.R3X.text: No conclusion when $\ell=1$; the idea is comparison with a geometric sequence.

HW5.1a.label: Problem 1(1)
HW5.1a.text: $A,B$ nonempty bounded. Prove $A\cup B$ is bounded, $\sup(A\cup B)=\max\{\sup A,\sup B\}$, $\inf(A\cup B)=\min\{\inf A,\inf B\}$. What about $A\cap B$?

HW5.1b.label: Problem 1(2)
HW5.1b.text: If $\sup A=\inf B$, prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $a\in A$, $b\in B$ with $b-a<\varepsilon$.

HW5.1c.label: Problem 1(3)
HW5.1c.text: If $A\subseteq B$, prove $\inf B\le\inf A\le\sup A\le\sup B$.

HW5.2a.label: Problem 2(1)
HW5.2a.text: $A$ upper bounded, $B$ lower bounded. Prove $\sup A\le\inf B$ iff $a\le b$ for all $a\in A$, $b\in B$.

HW5.2b.label: Problem 2(2)
HW5.2b.text: If for every $a\in A$ there is $b\in B$ with $a\le b$, prove $\sup A\le\sup B$.

HW5.3.label: Problem 3(a)–(h)
HW5.3.text: Find max, min, sup, inf (if they exist): (a) $\{x\in\mathbb R:x>0,\,0<x^2-1\le2\}$ (b) same set in $\mathbb Q$ (c) $\{0,\frac12,\frac13,\dots\}$ (d) $\{\frac1n+(-1)^n\}$ (e) $\{5+\frac6n\}\cup\{7-8n\}$ (f) $\{1+(-1)^n+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}n\}$ (g) $\{\frac1{2^n}+\frac1{3^m}\}$ (h) $\{\frac{(-1)^{nm}}{2^{n+m}}\}$.

HW5.3b.label: Problem 3(b)
HW5.3b.text: Max, min, sup, inf of $B=\{x\in\mathbb Q: x\ge0,\ 0<x^2-1\le2\}$ in $\mathbb R$.

HW6.2.label: Problem 2
HW6.2.text: If $a_0\in A$ and $a\le a_0$ for all $a\in A$, prove $a_0=\sup A$ (a maximum is the supremum).

HW6.3.label: Problem 3
HW6.3.text: For $a<b$, find and justify $\sup$ and $\inf$ of $(a,b)\cap\mathbb Q$.

HW6.4b.label: Problem 4(b)
HW6.4b.text: Prove every nonempty lower bounded $T\subseteq\mathbb R$ has an infimum (use (a) and completeness).

HW6.4c.label: Problem 4(c)
HW6.4c.text: In any complete totally ordered set, every nonempty lower bounded set has an infimum (hint: sup of the set of lower bounds).

HW6.4e.label: Problem 4(e)(i)–(ii)
HW6.4e.text: $\sup(tA)=t\sup A$, $\inf(tA)=t\inf A$ for $t\ge0$; $\sup(tA)=t\inf A$, $\inf(tA)=t\sup A$ for $t<0$.

HW7.1ab.label: Problem 1(a)–(b)
HW7.1ab.text: Polar form of $\sqrt3+i$, $-1+i$, $-\sqrt3-i$ (argument in $[0,2\pi)$, sketch). Then compute $z_1z_2$ in polar form and check in Cartesian form.

HW7.1c.label: Problem 1(c)
HW7.1c.text: Explain geometrically what multiplying by $i$ does; by $-1$?

HW7.2.label: Problem 2(a)–(b)
HW7.2.text: (a) $(1+i)^{20}-(1-i)^{20}$. (b) How many distinct values does $i^n+i^{-n}$ take?

HW7.3a.label: Problem 3(a)
HW7.3a.text: State de Moivre's formula; compute $\left(\cos\frac\pi6+i\sin\frac\pi6\right)^8$ in $a+bi$ form.

HW7.3bc.label: Problem 3(b)–(c)
HW7.3bc.text: Find the third roots of unity, sketch them, explain the equilateral triangle; explain why $n$th roots are $n$ equally spaced points.

HW7.4c.label: Problem 4(c)
HW7.4c.text: Among $z$ with $|z-4i|=2$, which has the smallest and largest modulus?

HW7.5.label: Problem 5
HW7.5.text: Prove $d(z,w)=|\operatorname{Re}(z-w)|+|\operatorname{Im}(z-w)|$ is a distance on $\mathbb C$.

HW7.6a.label: Problem 6(a)
HW7.6a.text: Nonreal roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs: $\overline{z^k}=\bar z^k$, $\overline{p(z)}=p(\bar z)$, quadratic with roots $2\pm3i$.

HW7.6bc.label: Problem 6(b)–(c)
HW7.6bc.text: If $|z|=1$ then $\bar z=\frac1z$; if all $|z_j|=1$ then $|z_1+\dots+z_k|=\left|\frac1{z_1}+\dots+\frac1{z_k}\right|$.

HW8.1.label: Problem 1(a)–(d)
HW8.1.text: Discrete metric: (a) it's a metric (b) describe $B(x,r)$ for $0<r\le1$ and $r>1$ (c) every subset is open and closed (d) compare $B(x,1)$ and $D(x,1)$.

HW8.1b.label: Problem 1(b)
HW8.1b.text: Describe the discrete-metric ball $B_{d_{disc}}(x,r)$ for $0<r\le1$ and $r>1$.

HW8.4.label: Problem 4
HW8.4.text: If $a_n\to a>0$, then $a_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

HW8.5.label: Problem 5
HW8.5.text: If $a=\sup A$, there is a sequence in $A$ with $a_n\to a$ (use the $\varepsilon$-characterization).

HW8.6.label: Problem 6
HW8.6.text: If $a_n>0$ and $a_n\to0$, then $\{a_n\}$ has a maximum.

HW9.1a.label: Problem 1(a)
HW9.1a.text: Behavior of $\left(\frac{1+i}3\right)^n$, $(-i)^n$, $(1+i)^n$ using the geometric-sequence theorem.

HW9.2.label: Problem 2(a)–(d)
HW9.2.text: Limiting behavior of $\frac{n^4}{3^n}$, $\frac{n!}{4^n}$, $\left(\frac{2n+1}{3n-1}\right)^n$, $\frac n{2^n+(-1)^n}$ (ratio, root, comparison).

HW9.3.label: Problem 3
HW9.3.text: $a_n=\frac{1+n\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^n}$: decreasing, converges (MCT), limit via ratio criterion.

HW9.45.label: Problems 4–5
HW9.45.text: Recursive sequences $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{3+a_n}$ and $a_{n+1}=\frac12(a_n+\frac2{a_n})$: bounded, monotone, limit.

HW9.6b.label: Problem 6(b)
HW9.6b.text: Convergent $\Rightarrow a_{n+m}-a_n\to0$ for each fixed $m$. Converse? Where does the order of quantifiers matter?

P8.1.text: $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ nonempty, bounded above. Which is correct? (A real number is an upper bound iff it is $\ge\sup S$.)

P12.4.text: True or false: a subset of $\mathbb R$ that is not open is closed.
